column1: # TROVE - THE NATIONAL LIBRARY OF AUSTRALIA'S DIGITISED NEWSPAPERS. Tested 27 September 2026.
# David obtained an API key valid to December 2026 and asked whether it was any use here.
# *** THE HONEST ANSWER IS NO, AND THE NULL IS WELL CONTROLLED. *** Recorded rather than dropped,
# because "we tried Australia" is exactly the kind of thing a future reader would otherwise repeat.
# *** THE KEY IS NOT IN THIS REPOSITORY AND MUST NEVER BE. *** daviddef/TheLerena is PUBLIC and every
# file in data/ is published. The key was passed as an environment variable for the session and nothing
# more. Anyone repeating this needs their own, free, from the link in the source column.
# *** THE CONTROL IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. *** A zero for an Argentine-Uruguayan family in Australian
# newspapers is unsurprising and therefore uninformative - unless you first show the corpus COULD have
# carried them. It could: Australian papers covered South African racing heavily, which is the world
# Pablo Armando worked in. *** 11,500 hits *** for South African racing at Johannesburg, with headings
# like "SOUTH AFRICAN RACING MATTERS - JOHANNESBURG RACING FEES" (1914). The shelf is not empty; he is
# simply not on it.
# *** AND ONE TRAP WORTH MORE THAN THE SEARCH. *** "Brayley Bideford" returned two hits and both looked
# like the Devon family. Neither is. Trove treats a whole FAMILY NOTICES COLUMN as one article - the
# 1914 Adelaide Observer block runs to 14,464 characters - so two terms "co-occurring" can mean only
# that they were set in the same column of type on the same morning. In that one: "MRS. BRAYLEY, of
# Gladstone" is a bereavement card from South Australia, and the Bideford is a quite separate notice,
# "JAMES - at Hallsannery, Bideford, N. Devon". *** A CO-OCCURRENCE SEARCH AGAINST A CORPUS OF LONG
# COLUMNS IS NOT A CO-OCCURRENCE. *** Every multi-term hit below was opened before being believed.
